item.title: Changing contribution of a shared neighbourhood pattern to reported sexual and non-sexual violence against women and girls in Medell\'in, Colombia, 2018--2022
item.description: arXiv:2610.31741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: During the COVID-19 restrictions, notifications of violence against women and girls may have changed unevenly across neighbourhoods. We asked whether the contribution of a shared neighbourhood pattern changed over this period, and whether any change was common to sexual and non-sexual violence or specific to one. We analysed 46,390 suspected cases notified to the public-health surveillance system of Medell\'in, Colombia, across 285 neighbourhoods in 2018-2022. A Bayesian shared-component model with age-standardised expected counts allowed the loading of a common spatial field on each form of violence to differ between the pre-pandemic (2018-2019), restriction (2020-2021) and post-restriction (2022) periods. Across the urban communes, the shared field was generally higher where living conditions were poorer. During the restrictions, its loading increased by 0.26 (95% credible interval 0.16-0.37) for non-sexual violence and by 0.23 (0.09-0.37) for sexual violence, without clear evidence of a change in their ratio. Between neighbourhoods at the 90th and 10th percentiles of the shared field, the shared component's contribution to their risk ratio widened by about 36% for non-sexual and 31% for sexual violence. In 2022, the non-sexual loading remained 0.19 (0.07-0.31) above its pre-pandemic value, whereas the sexual-violence loading was close to its pre-pandemic level. The direction of these changes was retained among notifications from health institutions only and under alternative specifications. Twenty-five neighbourhoods had joint probabilities above 0.95 of both relative risks exceeding one in all five years. The contribution of the shared neighbourhood pattern increased for both outcomes during the restrictions and remained elevated in 2022 for non-sexual violence.
item.dc:creator: Tom\'as Rodr\'iguez-Taborda, Alejandra-Estefan\'ia Pati\~no-Hoyos, Sim\'on Ruiz-Mart\'inez, Johnatan Cardona-Jim\'enez

item.title: Hierarchical Absorbing Markov Chain Models for Pooling Sparse Combat Sequence Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.31787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By viewing tactics in no-gi Brazilian jiu-jitsu (NGJJ) as discrete states, we estimate the transition probabilities of tactical progression, while simultaneously exploring the effects of weight categories on these dynamics with a hierarchical absorbing Markov chain model. We further cluster the weight categories and borrow strength using the Ewens-Pitman attraction of Dahl, Day and Tsai. Random partitions allow us to explore the underlying groupings of these weight categories in terms of their transition patterns. The hierarchical structure enables us to obtain an overall mean estimate of the transition probability matrix along with the individual estimates of the weight categories. Through simulations we find that the proposed model is more flexible than hierarchical methods with no partition or fully-pooled alternatives while sacrificing very little efficiency under model misspecification. Applying this method to NGJJ, we found a back-take is the tactic most likely to lead to achieving submission across all weight categories. In addition, we discovered the lightest (66kg) and heaviest (99kg+) weight categories vary significantly from the others in long-term tactical progression.
item.dc:creator: Brigham Halverson, Matthew Heiner, Leonardo Lamas, Gilbert Fellingham

item.title: Proportion Outcomes in Interrupted Time Series Analysis: Why Both Boundedness and Autocorrelation Matter
item.description: arXiv:2610.31969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Background: Proportions are common in interrupted time series analysis (ITSA), but bounded outcomes and serial dependence require distinct modeling considerations. This article provides guidance on selecting and evaluating models for proportion outcomes. Methods: Two published healthcare ITSA studies were reanalyzed. The first examined weekly proportions near the boundaries of the unit interval using segmented linear regression. The second examined monthly proportions without reported assessment or adjustment for autocorrelation. Both were reanalyzed using models appropriate for their outcome distributions and temporal dependence. Results: In the first study, segmented linear regression produced six fitted values below zero, and 35 of 66 confidence intervals extended beyond the permissible outcome range. Fractional logistic regression constrained fitted means to the unit interval while accommodating zeros and ones. In the second study, beta autoregressive regression identified significant first-order serial dependence (rho1 = 0.263, 95% CI 0.093 to 0.432; P = .002). After adjustment, residuals showed no evidence of remaining autocorrelation (Ljung-Box Q12 = 15.59; P = .211). Conclusions: Boundedness and serial dependence are distinct considerations in ITSA of proportions. Accounting for autocorrelation does not ensure predictions remain within the permissible range, and modeling bounded outcomes does not ensure serial dependence is addressed. Investigators should assess both features and select models appropriate for the outcome distribution and temporal dependence.
item.dc:creator: Ariel Linden

item.title: Finite-horizon maintenance under geometric-process models: Quantifying model and decision uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2610.32108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometric process (GP) models are widely used for repairable systems whose inter-failure times evolve over successive failure-repair cycles. Maintenance decisions under GP models are often made with limited failure data and are subject to uncertainty in baseline selection and the resulting maintenance decision. Existing approaches typically rely on model ranking and plug-in estimates, which can understate uncertainty surrounding next-cycle replacement decisions. This paper develops a unified generalized-inference framework for finite-horizon, event-driven maintenance decision making under GP models. The proposed framework quantifies uncertainty in GP model parameters, cycle-specific reliability, hazard rate, one-cycle cost rate, and the associated optimal replacement time. For exponential and gamma baselines, the framework yields generalized confidence intervals through generalized pivotal quantities. For the Weibull baseline, it is implemented through a generalized fiducial approach. It also extends to a finite-sample discrimination procedure for quantifying baseline-selection uncertainty. Theoretical results establish the asymptotic validity of the proposed procedures and their interval estimates. Simulation study shows reliable finite-sample coverage for model parameters and nonlinear maintenance-relevant quantities, and satisfactory discrimination performance. A case study on aircraft air-conditioning failures shows that, in early cycles, replacement schedules with similar expected cost can imply materially different risk profiles, so a single plug-in recommendation may be misleading.
item.dc:creator: Wenhui Wu, Bingxing Wang, Wei Wang, Piao Chen

item.title: Mapping Academic Sports Analytics: A Content Analysis of JQAS and JSA
item.description: arXiv:2610.32354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sports analytics has expanded rapidly in professional sports and mainstream culture, yet defining its academic core remains a challenge. In this paper, we provide an empirical map of the academic sports analytics landscape based on a systematic content analysis of approximately 700 papers published in two leading dedicated journals, the Journal of Quantitative Analysis in Sports (JQAS) and the Journal of Sports Analytics (JSA), between the years 2005 and 2024. We classify each paper by sport discipline, mathematical method, and core research area, identify recurring themes, and examine macro trends. We find game tactics, player evaluation, team ranking, result forecasting, and tournament design to be the most studied research areas in sports analytics. We highlight selected papers in each area, illustrating the wide range of mathematical methods used and sports disciplines analyzed. Our work offers a comprehensive overview of the questions, methods, and disciplines that characterize the field, serving as a foundational reference for practitioners and researchers in sports analytics.
item.dc:creator: Adam Nathaniel

item.title: Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference for Extending Trial Findings to Target Populations
item.description: arXiv:2610.31915v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The CODIACS Vanguard randomized trial compared a depression care intervention with usual care for patients with persistent depressive symptoms following acute coronary syndrome. We assess whether its findings can be extended to broader patient populations represented by two cohorts constructed from the All of Us electronic health records. This extension is challenging when treatment effects vary across covariates whose distributions differ between trial and target populations. We develop Bayesian Propensity Score Predictive Inference (PSPI), an interaction-based outcome modeling framework that combines Bayesian additive regression trees for potentially high-dimensional covariates with natural cubic splines of the sampling propensity score. Two variants include a separate spline in the treatment effect component alone or in both the prognostic and treatment effect components. The spline components allow separate regularization of selection-related variation and thus improve potential outcome estimation within the observed range and allow an explicit extrapolation rule beyond their boundary knots under substantial covariate shift. An inverse Gumbel transformation of the sampling propensity score balances compression near zero and the extent of extrapolation. Simulation studies show that spline-based PSPI models outperform competing methods in the settings studied, achieving lower root mean squared errors and near-nominal coverage, particularly under substantial covariate shift. In the application, PSPI estimates larger intervention benefits in both target populations than the unadjusted trial estimate.
item.dc:creator: Jungang Zou, Joseph E. Schwartz, Roderick J. A. Little, Nathalie Moise, Qixuan Chen

item.title: When Statisticians Can Also Be AI Engineers, What Could We Build?
item.description: arXiv:2610.32105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Statistical software makes methods widely available. Good statistical work, however, often requires conversations that clarify the scientific question, how the data were collected, and what conclusions the evidence can support. Coding agents and reusable AI infrastructure create opportunities for statisticians to incorporate these processes into agentic tools for research, practice, and education. A review of agentic AI applications for data analysis and study design distinguishes general human participation from human interaction guided by statistical principles. We examine how statistical expertise can guide the design and evaluation of domain-specific interactive harnesses. Two practical entry points illustrate how statisticians can begin building: an implemented causal-consulting skill within an existing agent environment and Model Forge, a custom harness for interactive model and algorithm development. These design examples connect statistical principles to choices about context, memory, tools, and interfaces, and motivate evaluation of both computational correctness and the scientific consequences of interaction. We conclude with a broader interdisciplinary research agenda on adaptive human-agent interaction, including selective information acquisition, evolving user preferences, and evaluation under uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Ruoqing Zhu

item.title: Bias-aware meta-analysis: beyond fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses
item.description: arXiv:2610.32183v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Meta-analysis aims to synthesize multiple studies to obtain a summary estimate of a population parameter of interest. However, existing meta-analysis methods require strong assumptions that render them not robust to bias and heterogeneity of the studies. In particular, fixed-effect meta-analysis assumes a common parameter across the studies, whereas random-effects meta-analysis models heterogeneity as independent and identically distributed random effects, which still implies a common parameter marginally over the random effects. Due to their limitations, we propose a bias-aware meta-analysis framework that allows for heterogeneous studies with fixed, unknown biases. With no bias, our bias-aware meta-analysis reduces to fixed-effect meta-analysis; with a given bound on the bias, we can still use the fixed-effect meta-analysis point estimator and standard error, but we must inflate the critical value for confidence intervals from the standard normal quantile to a folded normal quantile. We recommend reporting the maximum bias for significance, the maximum value of the bias such that the confidence intervals exclude the null value. We propose a formal model checking procedure and recommend reporting the minimum bias for compatibility, the minimum value of the bias such that the bias-aware meta-analysis model is compatible with the observed data. We discuss the practical implementation of our method and, in particular, the approaches to calibrating the maximum bias for significance. We also compare our method with traditional fixed-effect and random-effects meta-analyses.
item.dc:creator: Mingxuan Zou, Peng Ding

item.title: Honest Inference for Synthetic Controls with Imperfect Fit: Time-Split Validity and the Choice of Anchor
item.description: arXiv:2610.32383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Synthetic controls are used for one treated unit that lies outside its donors' range, with a pre-treatment window too short for residual-based standard errors to be trusted. We propose inference that separates the periods used to fit the synthetic control from the periods used to assess its error. Weights are fitted on an early block of pre-treatment periods, and the gap on a later block calibrates the bias and the noise. The resulting interval has finite-sample coverage under an explicit restriction on how far the counterfactual may depart from the extrapolated pre-treatment gap, for any fitting rule that uses only the early block. The leading restriction bounds the curvature of the gap and leaves its slope free, and the breakdown curvature at which the interval first includes zero states how much extrapolation a conclusion needs. We show when drift bounds calibrated from donor placebos are valid and how to allow for serial dependence. In simulations, conventional intervals undercover when the treated unit drifts from its donors, while the proposed interval covers whenever its restriction holds and the noise is serially independent. Re-analyses of three classic applications show that some well-known conclusions rest on far stronger extrapolation than others.
item.dc:creator: Rok Spruk

item.title: Direct Simulation of Poisson and Newton Kernel Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2610.32506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Poisson kernel-based (PKB) distribution is a flexible and numerically convenient family on the unit sphere used for model-based clustering, uniformity testing, and directional data analysis. Available random variate generators rely on rejection from a von Mises-Fisher, angular central Gaussian, or projected Saw envelope and therefore require a rejection loop, tuning or root-finding, or a univariate setup phase. We show that none is needed. A uniformly random line through the interior point $\rho\mu$ meets the sphere in two points; selecting one with probability proportional to the opposite segment length returns exactly the target density. The sampler is exact, rejection- and tuning-free, uses one uniform direction and one Bernoulli draw, and costs $O(d)$ operations. We place the distribution in the power-Saw family of densities proportional to $\|x-\rho\mu\|^{-\xi}$ and show that, for $d\geq3$, the same construction is exact for one further exponent. This introduces the Newton kernel-based (NKB) distribution, whose normalizing constant is identically one. Across a wide grid of dimensions, concentrations, and sample sizes, the direct sampler is faster than the better of two previously recommended methods in every case, with the largest gains at moderate concentration.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Sablica, Kurt Hornik

item.title: Efficient Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Multiple Membership Linear Mixed Models, with an Application to Educational Value-Added Assessments
item.description: arXiv:1403.7644v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The generalized persistence (GP) model, developed in the context of estimating ``value added'' by individual teachers to their students' current and future test scores, is one of the most flexible value-added models in the literature. Although developed in the educational setting, the GP model can potentially be applied to any structure where each sequential response of a lower-level unit may be associated with a different higher-level unit, and the effects of the higher-level units may persist over time. The flexibility of the GP model, however, and its multiple membership random effects structure lead to computational challenges that have limited the model's availability. We develop an EM algorithm to compute maximum likelihood estimates efficiently for the GP model, making use of the sparse structure of the random effects and error covariance matrices. The algorithm is implemented in the package GPvam in R statistical software. We give examples of the computations and illustrate the gains in computational efficiency achieved by our estimation procedure.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Computational Statistics & Data Analysis, Volume 59, March 2013, Pages 13-27
item.dc:creator: Andrew T. Karl, Yan Yang, Sharon L. Lohr

item.title: Avoiding Bias Due to Nonrandom Scheduling When Modeling Trends in Home-Field Advantage
item.description: arXiv:1806.08059v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing approaches for estimating home-field advantage (HFA) include modeling the difference between home and away scores as a function of the difference between home and away team ratings that are treated either as fixed or random effects. We uncover an upward bias in the mixed model HFA estimates that can arise when the schedule -- and thus the random effect design matrix -- depends on team strengths, and explore why the fixed effects model is not subject to the same bias. Intraconference HFAs and standard errors are calculated for each of 3 college sports and 3 professional sports over the 2000-2017 seasons and then fitted with conference-specific slopes and intercepts to measure the potential linear population trend in HFA.
item.dc:creator: Andrew T. Karl

item.title: Visualization Supporting Talent Portrait Generation:an Empirical Study
item.description: arXiv:2307.02731v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In current era of scientific and technological advancements,the importance of talent resources is increasingly highlighted.This article will attempt to summarize the academic trajectories and successes of numerous researchers from both past and present,aiming to reproduce the correlation between their personal development and academic output.This article proposes a framework of academic data collection,then use the framework to visualize numerous scientists research accomplishments,collaborative partners,and research inheritance.The article additionally posited a range of scholarly indices designed to quantitatively assess the impact of scientists.

item.title: Universal Inference for Testing Calibration and Specification of Mean Estimates within the Exponential Dispersion Family
item.description: arXiv:2510.23821v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Calibration of mean estimates is a crucial property in many applications, particularly in actuarial decision-making. Tests of mean-calibration are often performed under the assumption that the estimated means correctly preserve the ordering of the corresponding population means. In this paper, we first consider the classical Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT) within the Exponential Dispersion Family (EDF), and we show that applying likelihood-based methods to test mean-calibration within the EDF requires a strong ordering assumption on the mean estimates. This assumption makes the null hypothesis of the mean-calibration test equivalent to the correct specification of the mean estimates. Next, we investigate the framework of universal inference for testing mean-calibration and mean-specification, and the relationship between the tests. We develop a sub-sampled split LRT within the EDF that provides finite-sample guarantees with universally valid critical values. We investigate type I error, power, and e-power of the sub-sampled split LRT and compare its performance with that of the classical LRT. We also propose a novel test statistic based on a sub-sampled split $L_q$-likelihood ratio test (L$q$RT) to enhance the performance of the statistical test. Numerical results demonstrate that universal inference based on the sub-sampled split LRT and sub-sampled split L$q$RT provides an attractive alternative to the classical LRT within the EDF, achieving high power for detecting miscalibration and misspecification in medium- and large-sized samples.
item.dc:creator: {\L}ukasz Delong, Mario W\"uthrich

item.title: Women and the Nobel Prize in the sciences: an update to 2026
item.description: arXiv:2610.18592v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Every October, the Nobel Prizes in Physics, Chemistry, Physiology or Medicine and Economic Sciences are announced, with one to three prizes in each discipline. Of the 769 Laureates (since 1901) in these four disciplines only 4% are women (30 Laureates). In 2026, there are eight Laureates within these disciplines and they are all men. Based on historical data across four fields and a Bayesian hierarchical model, we update the 8 year old model on bias in Nobel Prizes and confirm the gender gap, with exceedingly large confidence.
item.dc:creator: Per Lunnemann, Liselotte Jauffred

item.title: Bayesian ACCESS for Understanding Latent Epidemic Trajectories from Publicly Released Suppressed Data: Application to U.S. Opioid-related Overdose Mortality
item.description: arXiv:2608.09103v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Publicly released health statistics play a central role in characterizing temporal trends and identifying structural changes in population health. However, disclosure limitation through suppression of small cell counts, as implemented in systems such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wide-ranging ONline Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER), produces partially observed count data that complicate statistical inference. These challenges are particularly acute for rare outcomes and subgroup analyses, where suppression is widespread and varies across geographic regions, demographic populations, and time. We propose Bayesian ACCESS (Autoregressive Change-point and Clustering Estimation for Suppressed Count Series), a Bayesian hierarchical framework for inference on latent epidemic trajectories and their structural changes from disclosure-limited health statistics. The proposed model directly represents suppressed count data through a suppression-aware observation model, jointly infers multiple temporal change points and latent trajectories, and borrows information across related geographic and demographic populations while preserving meaningful heterogeneity. We apply Bayesian ACCESS to opioid-related overdose mortality data from CDC WONDER for U.S. states from 1999 to 2024. The analysis identifies distinct subgroup-specific epidemic trajectories and structural changes that would be difficult to characterize using publicly released health statistics without explicitly accounting for data suppression and efficiently borrowing information across subgroups.
item.dc:creator: Jiahao Cao, Kehe Zhang, Cici Bauer

item.title: The Geometry of Existence and Uniqueness of Maximum Likelihood Estimation in Categorical Response Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.08100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Nonexistence of the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) under separation is treated as a solved problem for binary logistic regression and as a scattered collection of model-specific results everywhere else. We show that it is one phenomenon with one criterion. In a latent polyhedral categorical response model, every observed outcome corresponds to a polyhedral event in latent variables whose faces shift linearly with the parameter. Random-utility choice, cumulative-link, ranking, multivariate binary and ordinal, sequential, adjacent-category logit, and fixed-score stereotype models belong to this family. The likelihood sees each observed factor only through the columns of its threshold map, the structure vectors. A finite MLE exists if and only if the pooled structure vector set has overlap. Sufficiency requires only continuity, necessity requires only strictly threshold-increasing probabilities, and neither likelihood concavity, exchangeability, nor full design rank is needed. Positive strictly log-concave latent densities and threshold-identifiable polyhedra then yield uniqueness on the estimable span. A single linear program determines whether overlap holds, and convex cone geometry measures the dimension of separation. An application using cumulative-link models for willingness to share health data identifies observations and model terms associated with nonexistence and illustrates how the diagnostics inform model revision and sensitivity analysis.
item.dc:creator: Lukas Sablica, Kurt Hornik, Thomas Rusch

item.title: Score-optimized copula coupling for multivariate ensemble post-processing
item.description: arXiv:2610.24591v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Statistical post-processing can calibrate the individual components of an ensemble forecast but may also distort relationships between forecast dimensions. This paper proposes Score-Optimized Copula Coupling, which rearranges calibrated forecast samples according to an optimized dependence structure to restore potentially lost dependencies. We assess fixed and adaptively updated versions using wind-speed and temperature forecasts. In the variable-specific spatial case studies, all versions significantly outperform the strongest benchmarks, with improvements of 1.08-2.02 percent in energy score and 5.45-7.97 percent in variogram score. A third case study at 24 co-located stations shows that one optimized structure can represent both spatial and inter-variable relationships. The largest energy and variogram score improvements are 3.98 and 3.69 percent for spatial dependence and 1.16 and 1.06 percent for inter-variable dependence; all are statistically significant. Additional calibration terms improve covariance representation but can reduce gains in the other scores.
item.dc:creator: M\'aria Lakatos
